newsitem.title: USA: Republicans mull new request on campaign funds.
newsitem.headline: Republicans mull new request on campaign funds.

text.p: Republicans might file a new request for an independent investigation of foreign contributions to the Democratic Party, but for now will rely on Congress to probe the funding, two Republican senators said Sunday.

Attorney General Janet Reno rejected Friday a request for an independent counsel from Sen. John McCain of Arizona and four Republican House members, saying their letter had not offered enough specific evidence that any high-ranking person covered by the law had committed a crime.
"Maybe there'll be another request to her that'll be even more specific than Sen. McCain's letter," Sen. Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said on NBC television's "Meet the Press."
"I hope she does reconsider," he said.
But Nickles and McCain, who has led campaign finance reform efforts, said the focus would now shift to Congress to probe the controversial contributions.

Speaking on ABC's "This Week," McCain said he respected Reno's decision, but disagreed there was no need for an independent investigator separate from the Justice Department's task force looking into the campaign funding.
"We will place more emphasis on congressional hearings, which are not always the most non-partisan way of addressing these issues, unfortunately," McCain said.
He said the biggest question was whether contributions from the Lippo Group, an Indonesian conglomerate, had influenced U.S. policy toward Indonesia.

He cited what he called Clinton's "180-degree turn" from criticising the Indonesian government's abuses of human rights when he was a presidential candidate in 1992 to calling recently for the sale of nine fighter planes to Indonesia.
White House officials have insisted that despite their contacts with Lippo Group head James Riady, the United States has kept pressure on Indonesia to improve its human rights record.

"If Mr. Riady's meetings with the president of the United States resulted in changes in American foreign policy ... then that could have very serious implications," McCain said, declining to predict what steps might be taken if Clinton was found to have traded money for changes in foreign policy.
Retiring Democratic Sen. Bill Bradley of New Jersey dismissed complaints about the switch in Clinton's views on Indonesia, saying candidates often change their views once in office.
Both senators repeated their calls for sweeping changes in campaign finance rules to limit the amount and sources of money for political campaigns.
